blocks.heading: Favor or righteousness; Cheshvan after Tishrei

paragraphs.text: The Rav opens with the passuk that Noach found favor in Hashem's eyes. The Midrash reads chen, favor, as chinam, free: Noach was saved as a gift, not for his deeds. Yet the next passuk calls him a tzaddik. He then notes that Cheshvan has begun, while people still long for the sweet prayers of Tishrei.

Touching lightly on Kabbalah, the Rav explains that each month is governed by one of twelve arrangements of the four-letter Name, each drawn from a passuk. Cheshvan's, vav-hei-hei-yud, comes from Devarim: 'u'dvash', ending the passuk about the land flowing with milk and honey, then the first letters of 'hayom hazeh Hashem', which opens a new passage. It is the only combination that runs from one passuk into another.

blocks.heading: Bringing Tishrei's honey into the month of Bul

paragraphs.text: To explain this, the Rav describes Tishrei as a month of honey: our bread was dipped in honey, and our tefillos were sweet as we called Hashem the merciful Father who remembers His creations for life. 'Av HaRachaman' has the gematria of 'dvash', 306, so in Tishrei Hashem appears as sweetness.

Cheshvan, called Bul in Tanach, is the opposite: the month of decay, when leaves fall and what spring built falls apart. So the combination joins 'u'dvash' to 'hayom hazeh', where Rashi says the mitzvos should be new in one's eyes every day. The Rav says Tishrei's renewal and resolutions must be carried into Cheshvan, and then the Torah will feel new every day.

blocks.heading: Zichronos: why Noach needed to be remembered

paragraphs.text: Parshas Noach seems a parsha of decay, but the Rav says it is not. In Zichronos on Rosh Hashanah we say that we are tiny in Hashem's creation, yet He remembers every creature. Its first passuk is about Noach: Hashem remembered him and the animals in the Teivah, passed a wind over the earth, and the waters receded. So we ask Him to remember us.

The Rav asks why Noach needed to be remembered 'with love'. The plan was told to Noach 120 years earlier: build a Teivah, enter with the animals, and emerge as the nucleus of a new world. Without that love, he says, Hashem would have left them stranded like a spaceship in space.
The Mabul wiped out everything that recalled the old world, even the topsoil. Rashi explains 'ach Noach' as a groan: Noach was late serving the lion its meal, and the lion wounded and crippled him.

The Ramban explains that the Teivah was a great miracle: a box of three hundred by fifty by thirty amos could not naturally hold every species, nor could Noach feed them all on time. If Hashem helped him beyond nature, why was the lion permitted to injure him?

The Ibn Ezra answers those who ask where Noach found meat for the lion: a lion can eat straw. The Rav objects from Chazal that Noach brought each creature its own diet, twigs for the elephant and glass for a bird that eats glass.
Rashi adds that Hashem promised the food would not rot, so meat too would have stayed fresh. Why, then, did Noach fail to feed the lion?

blocks.heading: When Mashiach comes: the lion will eat straw

paragraphs.text: Recalling a song mothers sang about the coming of Mashiach, the Rav says that era already existed before Adam's sin, when people were meant to live forever in a perpetual spring and could pet lions and tigers that ate grass.
So it will be again, as Yeshayahu describes the wolf with the sheep and the lion eating straw. The Ramban explains that predators were meant to be gentle and became vicious only through Adam's sin.

blocks.heading: Man's deeds rule creation; Noach's portion

paragraphs.text: Hashem created man to rule, at the control center of the universe. The Midrash says a mitzvah perfects creation and an aveirah spoils it; these are its rules, like the laws of physics. When man is a tzaddik the animals are benign and the earth gives plenty; when he is a rasha, the opposite.

Rashi says even the animals of the Mabul's generation were corrupt. Since animals have no choice, the Rav explains that man's immorality was mirrored in them. Chazal say the earth too misbehaved, so even its top layer was wiped away.

Noach and his family were tzaddikim, so the part of creation under his control, the animals that came to the Teivah, stayed pure. His share of the land was Eretz Yisrael, where, the Gemara says, no Mabul fell.

Adam's sin spoiled the perfect world Hashem made, until ten generations later even animals and soil were corrupt. Noach, his family and his animals were to be the embryo of a new world. So the Teivah was no ship but a Beis HaMikdash: like the Mishkan it had halachos and exact dimensions, and as heaven on earth it was exempt from the Mabul. Inside lived a society of tzaddikim, people and animals, as perfect as Adam before the sin.

blocks.heading: Why the lion eats meat; Cham's sin

paragraphs.text: Would a lion eat meat there? The Rav asks why the lion eats meat at all. Life, he explains, is heavenly: we live not on bread but on the word of Hashem within it, which we extract. A tzaddik extracts it easily and eats little; Rav Nachum of Chernobyl ate very little bread yet was heavy, and the Ba'al Shem Tov said he was nourished by answering Amen yehei shmei rabba.

A sheep draws life from grass, but the cruel, unclean lion cannot, so it needs concentrated food, meat. In the Teivah's utopia the lion needed none, and Noach brought only plants. But, as Rashi explains, cohabitation was forbidden in the Teivah, and Cham, the raven and the dog disobeyed and were cursed.

blocks.heading: Digression on the curse of Cham

paragraphs.text: In a digression, the Rav contrasts the passuk's account of Noach cursing Cham with the outlook of a society that does not live by the Torah. He stresses that Torah Jews do not look down on others, since all men are created equal, but holds that the curse remains until Mashiach comes.

blocks.heading: The utopia lost, and Hashem's love for Noach

paragraphs.text: Cham's sin spoiled the Teivah as Adam's spoiled Eden. The curse returned and touched even Noach, who came out no longer holy and planted a vineyard; the Eitz HaDaas, the Rav notes, was a grapevine. Now the lion needed meat, Noach had none, and the lion wounded him.

Having spoiled Hashem's plan, they no longer merited miracles, and Hashem could have left them stranded. He remembered Noach with love because from him would come Avraham Avinu and the Jewish nation, who will bring the world to its perfection.

blocks.heading: Encouragement for Cheshvan: the third world

paragraphs.text: So in Zichronos we ask Hashem to spare us as He spared Noach, for what will come of us. Hashem, the Rav says, makes three tries: two Batei Mikdash fell and the third will stand; the worlds of Adam and Noach were spoiled, and the third will not be.
The Mabul came in Cheshvan. Disappointed with what Tishrei achieved, we take encouragement from the sedra, which ends with the birth of Avraham Avinu.
